title: Laundry Room Organization Jars: What to Store in Them and What to Keep Locked Away
seoTitle: Laundry Room Organization Jars: Smart and Safe Uses
excerpt: Laundry room organization jars: use clear, labeled jars for clothespins, dryer balls, buttons and pocket finds, and keep detergent and pods in original containers in a high, closed cabinet.
imageCaption: An empty ribbed glass jar with a round wooden lid and a faceted clear knob. Photo: Sesoris product catalog.
content: The smartest **laundry room organization jars** hold the small, safe things that usually scatter across a laundry room: clothespins, wool dryer balls, spare buttons and safety pins, coins and hair ties found in pockets, mesh bags and lint you clear from the dryer. Jars look tidy on an open shelf and make small items easy to grab. Detergents, pods and other laundry chemicals are a different story. Child safety guidance says to keep them in their original, labeled containers, out of sight and reach, ideally in a high, locked cabinet, so plan your jars around everything else.

Glass and clear jars have become a favorite way to style a laundry room, and it is easy to see why. A row of matching jars on a shelf above the washer looks calm and organized. The problem is that many photos online show detergent powder and colorful pods decanted into open jars on a counter, which is exactly what safety experts warn against. This guide explains what jars are good for in a laundry room, what should stay in its original packaging, how to choose and place jars, and how to build a laundry room that is both pretty and safe.
## What Jars Are Good For in a Laundry Room
Jars work best for small, loose items that otherwise end up in a pile on top of the dryer.

- **Clothespins and clips** for hanging delicates or air-drying.
- **Wool dryer balls** between loads.
- **Spare buttons, safety pins and a small sewing kit** for quick repairs.
- **Pocket finds** such as coins, hair ties, lip balm and receipts, so nothing goes through the wash twice.
- **Small mesh laundry bags** for socks and delicates, rolled up.
- **Clothing tags, stain stick caps and small tools** that would otherwise roll away.
- **Dryer lint**, if you want to save it for craft projects or kindling.
Each of these is light, non-toxic and easy to see through clear glass. A shelf of labeled jars for these items keeps the work surface clear for folding.
## What Should Stay in Its Original Container

The American Academy of Pediatrics advises keeping laundry products in their original containers with the original label on them, closing them tightly when not in use, and putting them away out of sight and reach of children and pets. It says a high, locked cabinet is best, and advises against storing products on top of the washer and dryer or in storage drawers under laundry machines ([HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/Pages/Laundry-Room-and-Detergent-Safety.aspx)).

The same page warns that brightly colored single-load detergent packets can look like candy or gummy treats to children, and that packets dissolve quickly when they touch water, wet hands or spit. It advises not removing a packet from its original container until you are ready to put it in the washing machine. If a child gets the contents of a packet in their mouth or eye, the page says to call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.
That means the following are better kept in their original packaging:

- **Detergent pods and packets**
- **Liquid and powder detergent**
- **Bleach and stain removers**
- **Fabric softener and scent boosters**
- **Spray bottles of any cleaning product**
A clear jar full of pods on an open shelf is the opposite of what this guidance recommends. Keep these products together in a closed, high cabinet, and use jars for the safe items in the list above.
## Jar Uses at a Glance

| Item | Jar or original container? | Where to keep it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clothespins and clips | Jar | Open shelf near the drying rack |
| Wool dryer balls | Jar or basket | Shelf next to the dryer |
| Buttons, safety pins, sewing kit | Small jar with a lid | Shelf at eye level |
| Coins and pocket finds | Small jar | Next to where you sort laundry |
| Mesh laundry bags | Wide jar or bin | Shelf near the hamper |
| Detergent pods and packets | Original container | High, closed or locked cabinet |
| Liquid or powder detergent | Original container | High, closed or locked cabinet |
| Bleach, stain removers, sprays | Original container | High, closed or locked cabinet |
## Choose the Right Jars
Not every jar suits a laundry room. Think about the items, the space and who uses the room.

- **Clear glass** makes contents easy to see and looks good on open shelves. It is heavier and can break, so keep glass jars on stable shelves rather than on top of a vibrating machine.
- **Clear plastic** is lighter and less likely to break. It is a good choice for lower shelves or homes with young children.
- **Wide mouths** make it easy to grab clothespins or dryer balls with one hand.
- **Lids** keep dust and lint out. A lid with a gasket ring closes more snugly.
- **Matching shapes** look calmer than a mix of random jars, and they line up neatly on a shelf.

## Plan Where the Jars Go
Jars look best and work best when they have a clear home.

1. **Clear the room first.** Take everything off the shelves and the top of the machines.
2. **Sort into three groups:** items for jars, products for the closed cabinet and items that belong elsewhere in the house.
3. **Measure the shelf.** Note the depth and the height between shelves so jars fit with room for your hand.
4. **Put jars at the height you use them.** Clothespins near the drying rack, pocket finds near the sorting area and sewing supplies at eye level.
5. **Keep the top of the washer and dryer clear.** Vibration can walk jars to the edge, and the AAP advises against storing laundry products there.
A single shelf above the machines often holds everything that should go in jars. Our [laundry room shelving ideas](/blog/laundry-room-shelving-ideas) show more ways to add shelf space.
## Label Every Jar
Even clear jars benefit from labels. Labels tell everyone in the home what goes where, which keeps the system working after the first week.

- **Use simple words**, such as "Pins," "Buttons," "Dryer balls" and "Pocket finds."
- **Put labels on the front** at the same height on every jar.
- **Choose waterproof labels** in a room where things can get damp.
- **Add a label to the shelf edge** too, so the jar always goes back to the same spot.
Our [free printable storage bin labels](/blog/free-printable-storage-bin-labels) and [label organizer](/blog/label-organizer) guides have more ideas for labeling systems.
## The Pocket Jar Habit
One of the most useful jars in any laundry room is a pocket jar. Before clothes go in the washer, empty every pocket into it.

- **Coins, keys, hair ties and lip balm** all go in the jar.
- **Paper receipts and tissues** go in the trash, so they do not shred and stick to a whole load.
- **Check the jar once a week** and return things to their owners.
A pocket jar also helps catch items that can damage the machine or stain clothes. It turns sorting laundry into a quick routine instead of a surprise after the cycle.
## A Lint Jar Next to the Dryer

Cleaning the lint screen is one of the most important laundry habits. The AAP says to clean the lint trap after each use to help prevent fires, and notes that clogged lint traps are a common cause of house fires ([HealthyChildren.org](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/Pages/Laundry-Room-and-Detergent-Safety.aspx)).

- **Keep a small lidded jar or bin next to the dryer** so clearing the screen is quick and lint does not end up on the floor.
- **Empty the lint container regularly** into the trash.
- **Keep the lint container away from heat sources**, and never store it on top of a running dryer.
A dedicated container makes the habit easier, which is the whole point of organizing.
## Keep Laundry Products in a Closed Cabinet
Once the jars are in place, set up the cabinet that will hold the products that should stay in their original containers.

- **Choose the highest closed cabinet** in the laundry room.
- **Add a cabinet lock** if young children live in or visit the home.
- **Keep products upright** in their original containers, with lids tightly closed.
- **Group by use**, such as washing, stain treatment and fabric care.
- **Close and lock the laundry room door** when you leave, as the AAP suggests for homes with curious young children.
If your laundry room has no closed cabinet, consider adding one. Our [laundry room cabinet ideas](/blog/laundry-room-cabinet-ideas) cover wall cabinets for small spaces.

Jars need a stable shelf. In a laundry room without one, a small freestanding unit works well.

## Make Room for Sorting and Hampers
Jars handle the small stuff, but a laundry room also needs a place for dirty clothes waiting to be washed.

Our [laundry room organization tips](/blog/laundry-room-organization-tips) cover sorting systems for whole families.
## Style Jars Without Losing Function
Jars are often used to make a laundry room look nicer. A few simple rules keep them practical.

- **Limit the number of jars.** Five or six well-chosen jars look better than a crowded shelf.
- **Repeat one material and lid style** across the set.
- **Leave space between jars** so they are easy to lift out.
- **Mix jars with one or two baskets** for bigger items.
- **Keep a plant or a small print** on the shelf if you want a decorative touch, rather than filling jars with products that belong in a cabinet.
## Small Laundry Rooms and Closets
In a laundry closet, space is tight and jars need to earn their place.

- **Use the wall above the machines** for one narrow shelf of jars.
- **Choose small jars** for buttons, pins and pocket finds, and hang mesh bags on a hook.
- **Put products in a closed cabinet** or a lidded box on the highest shelf.
- **Keep the floor clear** with a slim hamper that folds flat.
See our [laundry closet ideas](/blog/laundry-closet-ideas) and [small laundry room organization](/blog/small-laundry-room-organization) for more compact layouts.
## Keep the Jars Clean and Useful
Laundry rooms collect lint, dust and the occasional splash, so jars need a little care to stay useful.

- **Wipe the outside of each jar** when you dust the shelf, so labels stay readable.
- **Empty and wash glass jars** every few months, and let them dry fully before refilling.
- **Check the gasket or lid** for lint buildup that stops it from closing properly.
- **Edit the contents.** If the button jar is overflowing with buttons nobody will use, keep a handful and pass the rest on.
- **Return pocket finds weekly** so the pocket jar never turns into a junk drawer.
## Set Up the Room for Everyone in the Home
A laundry room is often shared, so the system needs to make sense to every person who uses it.

- **Put the jars older children can use**, such as clothespins and the pocket jar, at a height they can reach safely.
- **Keep sewing supplies with sharp pins** a little higher if younger children use the room.
- **Post a short routine on the wall**, such as "Empty pockets, sort, wash, clean the lint screen."
- **Show everyone where products live** and remind them to close the cabinet after use.
When everyone knows where each item goes, the room stays organized without one person doing all the tidying.
## Common Laundry Jar Mistakes

- **Decanting detergent pods into open glass jars** on a counter or shelf within reach of children.
- **Storing jars on top of the washer or dryer**, where vibration can move them.
- **Using unlabeled jars**, so nobody knows what goes where.
- **Choosing jars that are too small** for dryer balls or mesh bags.
- **Filling every shelf with jars** and leaving no room for folding.
## Frequently Asked Questions
**Q: What can I put in jars in a laundry room?**

Small, non-toxic items such as clothespins, wool dryer balls, spare buttons and safety pins, coins and pocket finds, rolled mesh laundry bags and small tools. Jars keep these items visible and easy to grab.
**Q: Is it safe to put laundry pods in a glass jar?**

Child safety guidance advises against it. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends keeping laundry products in their original containers with the original label, tightly closed and out of sight and reach of children and pets, ideally in a high, locked cabinet.
**Q: Can I decant laundry detergent into a jar?**
The same guidance recommends keeping laundry products in their original, labeled containers. Use jars for non-chemical items instead, and keep detergent in a closed, high cabinet.
**Q: Where should laundry detergent be stored?**

In its original container with the lid tightly closed, out of sight and reach of children and pets. A high, locked cabinet is best, and the AAP advises against storing products on top of the washer and dryer or in drawers under laundry machines.
**Q: What kind of jars are best for a laundry room?**

Clear jars with lids are easiest to use. Glass looks good on stable shelves, while plastic is lighter and less likely to break. Wide mouths help with clothespins and dryer balls, and a lid with a gasket keeps out dust and lint.
**Q: How do I keep jars from falling off laundry shelves?**
Keep jars off the top of the machines, place them on a stable shelf with a liner or tray, leave space between them and keep heavier jars on lower shelves.
**Q: What is a pocket jar?**
A small jar where you empty every pocket before washing. It collects coins, keys, hair ties and lip balm so they do not go through the wash, and you can return items to their owners once a week.
**Q: Why should I clean the dryer lint trap after every load?**
The AAP says cleaning the lint trap after each use helps prevent fires, and that clogged lint traps are a common cause of house fires. A small container next to the dryer makes the habit easier.
## Final Thoughts

Jars can make a laundry room look calm and organized, as long as they hold the right things. Use them for clothespins, dryer balls, buttons, pins and pocket finds, label them clearly and keep them on a stable shelf. Keep detergents, pods and other laundry products in their original, labeled containers in a high, closed cabinet. That combination gives you a laundry room that looks good and is safe for everyone in the home.
